name: In-office professional bleaching

card.summary: Dentist-applied high-concentration peroxide whitening in a single visit; produces visible shade change, with common sensitivity and fading over months.
card.aka: Power bleaching, chairside whitening, Zoom, Opalescence Boost
card.note: Tooth sensitivity is commonly reported; results can fade and rebound within days to months.

quick.overview:
In-office bleaching is tooth whitening performed by a dentist or hygienist using a high-strength peroxide gel, often after the gums are protected with a barrier. It is among the most promoted cosmetic dental treatments and is discussed in looksmaxxing as a fast route to lighter teeth.

Wikipedia describes it as faster than take-home options, with shade improvements of roughly 2 to 7 shades and effects lasting months depending on habits. Nearly half the colour change from a one-hour session may be lost within a week, a rebound linked to tooth dehydration.
quick.mechanism: Hydrogen peroxide, or carbamide peroxide that releases it, generates free radicals that break down pigment molecules inside the tooth so that less light is absorbed. It targets intrinsic stain more than surface stain. Some systems add a blue-spectrum light, though a 2015 study cited by Wikipedia found no added benefit.
quick.risks: Reported tooth sensitivity ranged from 67 to 78 percent in cited in-office studies, lasting roughly 4 to 39 days. Peroxide at 10 percent or more can irritate gum tissue, and bonded restorations can be affected. Contraindications listed include pregnancy, breastfeeding, children under 16, untreated decay or gum disease and exposed dentine. In the EU, higher-strength products are limited to dental professionals.

lead: In-office professional bleaching is tooth whitening carried out by a dentist or hygienist using a high-concentration peroxide gel. The active agents are hydrogen peroxide and carbamide peroxide, which releases hydrogen peroxide on contact with water; the peroxide produces free radicals that break down pigment molecules so teeth reflect less light [1].

A typical in-office visit begins with an examination and cleaning, with the gums covered by a light-cured barrier. Wikipedia reports gels with 10 to 44 percent carbamide peroxide (about 3 to 16 percent hydrogen peroxide), and power bleaching with 25 to 38 percent hydrogen peroxide for 6 to 15 minutes of light exposure [1]. Branded systems are named in forum discussion, such as Zoom and Opalescence Boost.

Cited sources describe shade improvement of 2 to 7 shades, with colour that can fade and a partial early rebound; sensitivity is common [1]. No clinical studies are summarised here because no trial sources were available in this entry's research.

paras: According to Wikipedia, the dentist examines and cleans the teeth, protects the gums, and applies the gel, sometimes with a light source such as halogen, LED or plasma arc lamps, most in the blue spectrum [1]. Internal bleaching is a separate approach for root-canal-treated teeth and carries a risk of root resorption [1].

Wikipedia says light can enhance whitening without added sensitivity when used properly, but cites a 2015 study in which light activation did not improve results and likely raised tissue temperature [1].

Wikipedia describes in-office whitening as faster and more effective than take-home options, though that statement is tagged as needing medical citation [1]. Bleaching is described as working best on yellow teeth and least on grayish ones, with uneven results common [1].

Nearly half the colour change from a one-hour session may be lost within seven days, linked to dehydration of the tooth, and stains can return within months; retreatment every six to twelve months is mentioned [1].

Cited figures show 67 to 78 percent of in-office patients reporting sensitivity where hydrogen peroxide and heat were used, lasting roughly 4 to 39 days; potassium nitrate and fluoride toothpastes ease discomfort [1]. Hydrogen peroxide at 10 percent or more can damage tissue, and chemical burns often follow poorly fitting trays [1].

Other reported effects include increased enamel roughness and porosity, reduced composite bond strength, and temporary mercury release from amalgam [1]. The IARC found insufficient evidence that hydrogen peroxide is a human carcinogen [1]. Contraindications listed include age under 16, pregnancy or breastfeeding, untreated gum disease or decay, cracks or exposed dentine, and peroxide allergy [1].

In the EU, retail products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide, and up to 6 percent may only be provided by a certified dental professional to patients aged 18 or older [1]. The US FDA is cited as endorsing gels under 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or up to 16 percent carbamide peroxide for consumer products [1].
No studies found in the material gathered for this entry; Wikipedia summarises research on bleaching in general, as cited above [1].

timeline.event: Dr William Klusmeier introduced custom tray bleaching.[1]
Haywood and Heymann published support for custom-tray carbamide peroxide bleaching.[1]
